definition: A right to buy a company's shares at a fixed price (AMD's OpenAI warrant: $0.01 per share), usually vesting only when conditions are met. It costs the issuer no cash but dilutes existing shareholders.
The fall in existing owners' percentage stake when a company issues new shares, for example to pay for an acquisition or to settle a warrant.
A deal in which a chip vendor gives a customer money or equity (cash stakes, warrants, backstops) in exchange for a commitment to deploy a stated amount of its compute, often measured in gigawatts.
A non-binding document stating that parties intend to agree a deal on outlined terms; it can be dropped or rewritten before a definitive agreement, as NVIDIA's 2025 OpenAI LOI was.

A deal structure in which a buyer pays for a non-exclusive licence to a start-up's technology and hires its founders and engineers, while the start-up survives as a separate company; it can avoid formal merger review.

Antitrust screening of acquisitions by agencies such as the US FTC/DOJ (Hart-Scott-Rodino filings), the European Commission, the UK CMA and China's SAMR; reviews can take a year or more and can block deals, as with NVIDIA-Arm.
Minority investments by a company in start-ups, made for strategic as well as financial reasons; NVIDIA invests directly and through its NVentures arm.
Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure: the cash a company generates that it can return to shareholders, use for acquisitions or invest in other companies.
Prepaid usage that a cloud provider grants to start-ups (for example up to $350,000 at Google Cloud for AI-first start-ups) to win their workloads early.
A company training the largest general-purpose AI models (for example OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google DeepMind); each buys compute at gigawatt scale.
